questions.title: Ptosis can occur due to the following cause EXCEPT:
questions.question: Ptosis can occur due to the following cause EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Congenital lid muscle (levator) weakness is a recognised cause of ptosis, so it belongs among the true causes, not the exception.
explanations.B: Lid trauma, if it damages the levator or its aponeurosis, is a recognised cause of ptosis, so it belongs among the true causes, not the exception.
explanations.C: Third nerve paralysis removes the oculomotor nerve's supply to the levator palpebrae superioris and is a well-recognised cause of ptosis, so it belongs among the true causes, not the exception.
explanations.D: Orbicularis muscle paralysis is a fact about facial (7th) nerve palsy, and orbicularis is the lid-CLOSING muscle, not the lid-opening levator. Its paralysis causes lagophthalmos (failure to close the eye), not ptosis, so among these four options it is the one that does NOT cause ptosis. Ptosis instead follows failure of the lid-opening apparatus: the levator itself (congenital weakness, trauma) or its nerve supply (third nerve palsy), never the lid-closing orbicularis.

questions.title: Schirmer's test is used for diagnosing:
questions.question: Schirmer's test is used for diagnosing:

explanations.A: Schirmer's test, a strip of filter paper placed in the lower fornix to measure the length of wetting over five minutes, directly quantifies aqueous tear production and is the standard bedside test for dry eye. A short wetting length supports a diagnosis of aqueous-deficient dry eye. It is simple, inexpensive and widely used as a first-line diagnostic test.
explanations.B: Infective keratitis is diagnosed by slit-lamp examination, corneal scraping and culture, not by a tear-production test.
explanations.C: Corneal ulcers are diagnosed by slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining, not by a tear-production test.
explanations.D: Horner's syndrome is diagnosed by pharmacological pupil testing (such as apraclonidine or cocaine drops) and its associated ptosis/miosis/anhidrosis triad, not by a tear-production test.

questions.title: The most common cause of adult unilateral proptosis is:
questions.question: The most common cause of adult unilateral proptosis is:

explanations.A: Thyroid orbitopathy (thyroid eye disease) is overwhelmingly the commonest cause of proptosis in adults, whether the presentation is unilateral or bilateral, from autoimmune expansion of orbital fat and extraocular muscles. Even when proptosis appears unilateral, imaging often reveals subclinical bilateral orbital involvement, reflecting the same systemic autoimmune process. Its high prevalence relative to orbital tumours or infections is what makes it the single commonest cause in everyday practice.
explanations.B: Metastasis to the orbit is a recognised but much less common cause of adult proptosis than thyroid orbitopathy.
explanations.C: Orbital lymphoma is a recognised but much less common cause of adult proptosis than thyroid orbitopathy.
explanations.D: Meningioma (of the optic nerve sheath or sphenoid wing) is a recognised but much less common cause of adult proptosis than thyroid orbitopathy.

questions.title: Mucin layer of tears is secreted by:
questions.question: Mucin layer of tears is secreted by:

explanations.A: Conjunctival goblet cells secrete the tear film's innermost mucin layer, which allows the aqueous layer above it to wet the otherwise hydrophobic corneal epithelium evenly. Goblet cells are most concentrated in the bulbar and fornical conjunctiva. Their loss, as in vitamin A deficiency or cicatrizing conjunctival disease, destabilises the whole tear film and produces mucin-deficient dry eye.
explanations.B: The main lacrimal gland secretes the tear film's middle aqueous layer, not the mucin layer.
explanations.C: The meibomian glands secrete the tear film's outer lipid layer, which retards evaporation, not the mucin layer.
explanations.D: Accessory lacrimal glands (Krause and Wolfring) contribute basal aqueous tear secretion, not the mucin layer.

questions.title: Nasolacrimal duct opens in:
questions.question: Nasolacrimal duct opens in:

explanations.A: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior, not the superior, nasal meatus.
explanations.B: Tears drain from the lacrimal sac through the nasolacrimal duct, which opens into the inferior meatus of the nose, beneath the inferior nasal concha. This anatomical relationship is why nasal packing or turbinate surgery near the inferior meatus can occasionally injure the duct's opening. Endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy specifically targets this region when creating a new drainage passage.
explanations.C: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior, not the middle, nasal meatus.
explanations.D: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior nasal meatus, not directly into the nasopharynx.

questions.title: You can differentiate between a stye and a chalazion by:
questions.question: You can differentiate between a stye and a chalazion by:

options.A: The relation of the lesion to the caruncle.

explanations.A: The relation of a lid lesion to the caruncle (at the medial canthus) is not the feature used to distinguish a stye from a chalazion; both can occur anywhere along the lid, not specifically near the caruncle.
explanations.B: A stye (hordeolum externum) is an acute infection of a lash-follicle gland and so points at the lash-bearing lid margin itself, while a chalazion is a chronic granuloma of a deeper meibomian gland within the tarsal plate, away from the margin. This difference in position relative to the lid margin is the classic bedside distinguishing feature between the two. A stye is also acutely tender, while a chalazion is typically painless, reinforcing the same anatomical distinction.
explanations.C: The amount of discharge is not a reliable distinguishing feature between a stye and a chalazion; neither characteristically discharges externally.
explanations.D: Everting the eyelid is a general examination step, not the specific distinguishing feature between a stye and a chalazion.

questions.title: Chalazion is a chronic inflammatory granuloma of:
questions.question: Chalazion is a chronic inflammatory granuloma of:

explanations.A: A chalazion is a chronic inflammatory (lipo)granuloma of a meibomian gland, caused by retained sebaceous secretion provoking a sterile granulomatous reaction within the tarsal plate. It is not an infection, which is why it does not respond to antibiotics the way a stye does. Its treatment is instead incision and curettage, or intralesional steroid injection, for persistent lesions.
explanations.B: Zeis' gland inflammation, an acute infective process, produces a stye (hordeolum externum), not a chalazion.
explanations.C: Chalazion arises from a meibomian gland, not a sweat gland.
explanations.D: Wolfring's gland is an accessory lacrimal gland contributing basal tear secretion; its inflammation is not what defines a chalazion.

questions.title: Severe congenital ptosis, with no levator function can be treated by:
questions.question: Severe congenital ptosis, with no levator function can be treated by:

options.B: Surgical intervention between age of 6 till 10 years

explanations.A: Levator resection from the skin side needs measurable levator function to shorten; it is not the operation of choice when levator function is absent.
explanations.B: Deferring surgical intervention to age 6-10 is a timing consideration for milder ptosis, not the specific answer to how severe ptosis with no levator function should be treated.
explanations.C: When levator function is severely poor or absent, as in severe congenital ptosis, the levator cannot be usefully shortened by resection. A frontalis sling instead harnesses the frontalis muscle, via a sling material passed through the lid and anchored to the forehead, to lift the lid mechanically using brow movement. This bypasses the non-functioning levator entirely, which is why it is the standard operation for ptosis with no levator function.
explanations.D: Tarsorrhaphy narrows the palpebral fissure by suturing the lid margins together; it protects the cornea in lagophthalmos, but it does not correct or elevate a ptotic lid.

questions.title: If the palpebral fissure does not close completely during sleep, choose the wrong answer:
questions.question: If the palpebral fissure does not close completely during sleep, choose the wrong answer:

options.B: There is usually trigeminal nerve palsy
options.C: bell's phenomenon protects the cornea from ulceration
options.D: Lateral tarsorrhaphy is one of the management lines

explanations.A: Incomplete closure of the palpebral fissure during sleep is correctly called lagophthalmos, so this statement is true, not the wrong answer being sought.
explanations.B: Lagophthalmos is usually caused by facial (7th cranial) nerve palsy, paralysing orbicularis oculi, not trigeminal (5th cranial) nerve palsy, which affects sensation and mastication rather than eyelid closure. This statement is therefore the WRONG one among the four, which is exactly what the question asks for. Confusing the fifth and seventh cranial nerves in this context is a common source of error.
explanations.C: Bell's phenomenon (reflex upward eye rotation on attempted lid closure) does help protect the cornea from exposure in lagophthalmos, so this statement is true, not the wrong answer being sought.
explanations.D: Lateral tarsorrhaphy narrows the palpebral fissure and is a genuine management option for lagophthalmos, so this statement is true, not the wrong answer being sought.

questions.title: One of the following is not a test for dry eye:
questions.question: One of the following is not a test for dry eye:

explanations.A: The Hirschberg test estimates the angle of manifest strabismus from how far the corneal light reflex is displaced from the pupil centre, a test of ocular alignment, not of tear function. It has no role in diagnosing dry eye. Among these four options it is therefore the one that is NOT a dry-eye test, which is what the question asks for.
explanations.B: Rose Bengal corneal and conjunctival staining reveals devitalised epithelium and is a genuine dry-eye test, so it is not the exception being sought.
explanations.C: Schirmer's test measures aqueous tear production and is a genuine dry-eye test, so it is not the exception being sought.
explanations.D: Tear lysozyme level reflects one of the tear film's protective components and is used as a dry-eye test, so it is not the exception being sought.

questions.title: Defective lacrimal drainage can result in any of these conditions except:
questions.question: Defective lacrimal drainage can result in any of these conditions except:

explanations.A: Chronic dacryocystitis is a recognised consequence of defective lacrimal drainage (nasolacrimal duct obstruction with secondary sac infection), so it belongs among the genuine consequences, not the exception.
explanations.B: Trichiasis is a disorder of misdirected eyelash growth at the lid margin, caused by processes such as ulcerative blepharitis or trachomatous cicatricial entropion, entirely unrelated to the lacrimal drainage pathway. It is not a consequence of defective drainage, which is exactly what the question asks for. Trichiasis instead risks corneal abrasion from lash-corneal contact, a mechanical problem, not a tear-outflow one.
explanations.C: Stenosis of the lacrimal puncti is itself a form of defective lacrimal drainage and can be its cause or an associated finding, so it belongs among the genuine consequences, not the exception.
explanations.D: A mucocele of the lacrimal sac, from trapped, stagnant secretions behind an obstructed duct, is a recognised consequence of defective lacrimal drainage, so it belongs among the genuine consequences, not the exception.

questions.title: Congenital ptosis is characterized by:
questions.question: Congenital ptosis is characterized by:

explanations.A: Absent lid crease is a genuine sign of congenital ptosis, since the crease depends on normal levator aponeurosis attachment, which is deficient in levator dystrophy, so this option alone is incomplete.
explanations.B: Chin elevation, a compensatory posture to see beneath the drooping lid, is a genuine sign of congenital ptosis, so this option alone is incomplete.
explanations.C: Forehead corrugation, from frontalis overaction as the child tries to raise the lid, is a genuine sign of congenital ptosis, so this option alone is incomplete.
explanations.D: Congenital ptosis, from developmental dystrophy of the levator palpebrae superioris, characteristically shows all three signs together: an absent upper-lid crease, compensatory chin elevation, and forehead corrugation from frontalis overaction. Each sign reflects the same underlying mechanism, a weak or absent levator that the child compensates for using surrounding muscles and posture. Recognising the combination, rather than any single sign alone, is what makes the diagnosis clinically reliable.

questions.title: Treatment of hordeolum internum include all of the following except:
questions.question: Treatment of hordeolum internum include all of the following except:

explanations.A: Hot fomentation is a genuine, first-line treatment for hordeolum internum, helping the lesion localise and drain, so it belongs among the true treatments, not the exception.
explanations.B: Systemic or topical antibiotics are a genuine treatment for hordeolum internum when infection is significant, so they belong among the true treatments, not the exception.
explanations.C: Surgical evacuation (incision and drainage) is a genuine treatment for hordeolum internum that fails to resolve with conservative measures, so it belongs among the true treatments, not the exception.
explanations.D: Epilating the associated lash is the treatment for trichiasis (a misdirected-lash disorder), not for hordeolum internum, which is a suppurative meibomian-gland infection deeper in the tarsal plate, unconnected to any single lash. It has no established role in hordeolum management. Among these four options it is therefore the one that is NOT a hordeolum-internum treatment, which is what the question asks for.

questions.title: Trichiasis is caused by the following:
questions.question: Trichiasis is caused by the following:

explanations.A: Angular blepharitis, an infection localised to the lateral or medial canthal angle, is not the cause this key selects for trichiasis among these four options.
explanations.B: Hordeolum internum is a suppurative meibomian-gland infection, not a recognised cause of misdirected lash growth.
explanations.C: Ulcerative blepharitis's chronic lid-margin inflammation and scarring can distort the lash follicles and redirect lash growth inward, producing trichiasis. This mechanism, follicle-level scarring from chronic infective inflammation, is distinct from the conjunctival cicatricial-entropion route (as in trachoma) that also causes trichiasis. Both routes converge on the same end result, lashes rubbing against the cornea, but by different anatomical mechanisms.
explanations.D: Follicular trachoma is the acute, early conjunctivitis stage of trachoma; it is the later cicatricial (scarring) stage of trachoma, not the follicular stage itself, that classically produces entropion and trichiasis.

questions.title: Dry eye can be caused by all of the following except:
questions.question: Dry eye can be caused by all of the following except:

options.C: Atrophy of the accessory lacrimal glands.

explanations.A: Obstruction of the lacrimal puncti blocks tear drainage and so causes epiphora (excess tearing pooling on the eye), the clinical opposite of dry eye, rather than causing dryness itself. It is therefore not a recognised cause of dry eye, which is exactly what the question asks for. Confusing punctal obstruction (a drainage problem, too much retained tear film) with dry eye (a production or stability problem, too little functional tear film) is a common error.
explanations.B: Collagen vascular diseases, such as Sjögren's syndrome, cause aqueous-deficient dry eye through lacrimal gland infiltration, so this belongs among the true causes, not the exception.
explanations.C: Atrophy of the accessory lacrimal glands reduces basal aqueous tear secretion and is a recognised cause of dry eye, so it belongs among the true causes, not the exception.
explanations.D: Vitamin A deficiency causes mucin-deficient dry eye through goblet-cell loss, so it belongs among the true causes, not the exception.

questions.title: The lacrimal secretory system consists of the following parts except:
questions.question: The lacrimal secretory system consists of the following parts except:

explanations.A: The lacrimal gland is a genuine secretory structure (basal and reflex aqueous tears), so it belongs among the true parts of the secretory system, not the exception.
explanations.B: The accessory lacrimal glands are genuine secretory structures (basal aqueous tears), so they belong among the true parts of the secretory system, not the exception.
explanations.C: Goblet cells are genuine secretory structures (mucin), so they belong among the true parts of the secretory system, not the exception.
explanations.D: The lacrimal sac is a drainage (excretory) structure, receiving tears from the canaliculi and passing them to the nasolacrimal duct; it does not itself secrete any component of the tear film. Among the lacrimal gland, accessory lacrimal glands and goblet cells, all genuinely secretory, the sac is the one structure that belongs to the drainage pathway instead. This is exactly the exception the question asks for.

questions.title: The orbital portion of the lacrimal gland is responsible for:
questions.question: The orbital portion of the lacrimal gland is responsible for:

explanations.A: The main lacrimal gland's larger orbital portion, separated from the smaller palpebral portion by the levator aponeurosis, is chiefly responsible for reflex tear secretion, the sudden high-volume tearing triggered by irritation, emotion or corneal stimulation. Basal (resting) secretion instead depends mainly on the accessory lacrimal glands of Krause and Wolfring. This division between reflex and basal tearing, and between the gland's two parts, is a classic anatomical teaching point.
explanations.B: Basal tear secretion is mainly attributed to the accessory lacrimal glands, not to the orbital portion of the main lacrimal gland.
explanations.C: Mucin secretion is the role of conjunctival goblet cells, not of any part of the main lacrimal gland.
explanations.D: The orbital portion does have an established secretory role (reflex tearing), so "none of the above" is incorrect.

questions.title: A +ve regurge test is diagnostic of:
questions.question: A +ve regurge test is diagnostic of:

explanations.A: A positive regurgitation ('regurge') test, in which pressure over the lacrimal sac reflux material back through the puncti, confirms the sac is patent to the puncti but obstructed distally. This localises the block to the nasolacrimal duct, the segment between the sac and the nose, which is exactly the finding in chronic dacryocystitis. The test's mechanism, forcing trapped sac contents backward because the forward route is blocked, is what makes this localisation possible.
explanations.B: A canalicular obstruction, proximal to the sac, would prevent tears from reaching the sac at all, rather than producing the reflux a positive regurge test relies on.
explanations.C: Punctal occlusion, even more proximal than a canalicular obstruction, would likewise prevent tears from reaching the sac to be regurgitated.
explanations.D: Ectropion is an eyelid-margin malposition, unrelated to the mechanism a regurge test assesses.

questions.title: The mucin layer of the pre-corneal tear film is secreted by:
questions.question: The mucin layer of the pre-corneal tear film is secreted by:

explanations.A: The mucin layer of the pre-corneal tear film, its innermost component, is secreted by conjunctival goblet cells. This layer converts the hydrophobic corneal epithelial surface into one the aqueous layer above it can wet evenly, which is essential for a stable tear film and clear optics. Loss of goblet cells, as in vitamin A deficiency or cicatrizing conjunctival disease, destabilises the tear film even when aqueous production is normal.
explanations.B: The lacrimal gland secretes the tear film's middle aqueous layer, not the mucin layer.
explanations.C: The meibomian gland secretes the outer lipid layer, not the mucin layer.
explanations.D: Limbal stem cells maintain the corneal epithelium itself; they do not secrete any tear film layer.

questions.title: All the following statements about the pre-corneal tear film are correct except:
questions.question: All the following statements about the pre-corneal tear film are correct except:

options.A: It provides nutrition to the cornea.
options.B: It protects the cornea through its anti-bacterial effect.
options.D: It is not affected by deficiency of the Goblet cells.

explanations.A: The tear film does provide nutrition to the avascular cornea, so this statement is correct, not the exception being sought.
explanations.B: The tear film does protect the cornea through antibacterial substances such as lysozyme and lactoferrin, so this statement is correct, not the exception being sought.
explanations.C: The tear film does lubricate the corneal surface during blinking, so this statement is correct, not the exception being sought.
explanations.D: The tear film IS affected by deficiency of the goblet cells: their mucin layer allows the aqueous layer above it to wet the cornea evenly, and without it the whole tear film becomes unstable and breaks up prematurely. The claim that the tear film is 'not affected' by goblet-cell deficiency is therefore false, which is exactly the incorrect statement the question asks for. This is the same mucin-mediated stability principle that explains mucin-deficient dry eye.

questions.title: Investigations done in a case of epiphora include all of the following except:
questions.question: Investigations done in a case of epiphora include all of the following except:

options.A: Examination of the cheeks and face for scars.

explanations.A: Examining the cheeks and face for scars is a genuine part of the epiphora work-up, looking for previous trauma affecting the drainage pathway, so it belongs among the true investigations, not the exception.
explanations.B: Examining the lid margin for malposition (ectropion, punctal eversion) is a genuine part of the epiphora work-up, so it belongs among the true investigations, not the exception.
explanations.C: The Jones dye test, instilling fluorescein and tracking its passage through the drainage system, is a genuine part of the epiphora work-up, so it belongs among the true investigations, not the exception.
explanations.D: Fluorescein angiography images the retinal and choroidal vasculature after intravenous dye injection, an entirely different investigation from the lacrimal work-up despite sharing the name fluorescein. It has no role in investigating epiphora. Among these four options it is therefore the one that is NOT part of the epiphora work-up, which is what the question asks for.

questions.title: Complications of acute dacryocystitis include all of the following except:
questions.question: Complications of acute dacryocystitis include all of the following except:

explanations.A: Cavernous sinus thrombosis, from ascending spread via the ophthalmic veins, is a recognised complication of acute dacryocystitis, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.
explanations.B: Orbital cellulitis, from local spread of the infected sac, is a recognised complication of acute dacryocystitis, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.
explanations.C: A lacrimal fistula, from chronic discharge through the skin, is a recognised complication of acute dacryocystitis, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.
explanations.D: A squint (misalignment of the visual axes) is not a recognised complication of acute dacryocystitis, an infective process confined to the lacrimal sac and its immediate surroundings, unless it happens to spread to the orbit and secondarily affect an extraocular muscle, which is not what this option describes. Among cavernous sinus thrombosis, orbital cellulitis and fistula, all genuine spread complications, squint is the one that does NOT belong on this list. This is exactly the exception the question asks for.

questions.question: Contrast dacryocystography is indicated in the following conditions:

questions.question: Levator resection operation should be used in:

options.B: Moderate ptosis with good levator function
options.C: Moderate ptosis with poor levator function
options.D: Severe ptosis with poor levator function

explanations.A: Levator resection is not typically needed for mild ptosis with levator function present; milder cases may be managed more conservatively or with a smaller procedure.
explanations.B: Levator resection, shortening the levator palpebrae superioris to increase its lifting power, is the standard operation for moderate ptosis with good levator function: enough function must be present for shortening the muscle to produce a useful, predictable lift. This differs from frontalis sling, reserved for severe ptosis with absent or very poor function, where the levator itself cannot be relied on at all. Selecting the right operation for the right levator-function grade is central to achieving a good surgical outcome.
explanations.C: Moderate ptosis with poor levator function is more often managed with a larger resection or an alternative procedure tailored to the reduced function, not the standard resection this option implies for good function.
explanations.D: Severe ptosis with poor levator function is generally better served by a frontalis sling, not levator resection.

questions.title: Lagophthalmos occurs as a result of paralysis of:
questions.question: Lagophthalmos occurs as a result of paralysis of:

explanations.A: The 5th (trigeminal) cranial nerve governs facial sensation and mastication, not eyelid closure; its paralysis does not cause lagophthalmos.
explanations.B: Levator palpebrae superioris opens the eyelid; its paralysis causes ptosis, not lagophthalmos (a closure failure).
explanations.C: The 6th (abducens) cranial nerve controls the lateral rectus muscle for horizontal eye movement, not eyelid closure; its paralysis does not cause lagophthalmos.
explanations.D: Lagophthalmos, the inability to fully close the eyelids over the globe, results from paralysis of the 7th (facial) cranial nerve, which supplies orbicularis oculi, the lid-closing muscle. This is why Bell's palsy (facial nerve palsy) is the commonest cause of lagophthalmos in clinical practice. Because the cornea is left unprotected during attempted closure, exposure keratopathy and, if untreated, ulceration are the main risks.
explanations.E: Müller's muscle is a small accessory lid elevator whose loss of sympathetic tone (as in Horner's syndrome) produces a mild ptosis, not lagophthalmos.

questions.question: A 40-year-old female came to your clinic complaining of bilateral protrusion of her eyes. She gave a history of excessive sweating and weight loss. Examination revealed lid lag and lid retraction.

options.A: Hyperthyroidism is more in females than males.
options.B: Thyroid eye disease is improved by taking radioactive iodine.
options.C: Cornea is never affected in thyroid eye disease.
options.D: Glucocorticoids may be used in treatment of thyroid eye disease.

explanations.A: Hyperthyroidism (of which this vignette's excessive sweating and weight loss are features) is indeed more common in females, but that epidemiological fact is not the treatment-related statement this key selects as correct.
explanations.B: Radioactive iodine treats the underlying hyperthyroidism, but it is not established to reliably improve, and can in some cases transiently worsen, the orbital thyroid eye disease itself; this option overstates its ophthalmic benefit.
explanations.C: The cornea CAN be affected in thyroid eye disease, through exposure keratopathy from lid retraction, lagophthalmos and reduced blink rate, so a claim that it is "never" affected is false.
explanations.D: Systemic glucocorticoids are a genuine, recognised treatment for active, inflamed thyroid eye disease, used to control the orbital autoimmune inflammation directly rather than the systemic thyroid disease. This is distinct from the antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy used to correct the underlying hyperthyroidism itself. Recognising glucocorticoids' specific role in treating the orbital inflammation, not the thyroid gland, is the key teaching point here.

questions.title: A 60-year-old male patient came complaining of bilateral proptosis with impairment of central vision of his left eye and defective color vision especially red and green. Examination revealed afferent pupillary defect of his left eye. Vision was 6/24 in right eye and 2/60 in left eye. He gave history of thyroid eye disease.
questions.question: A 60-year-old male patient came complaining of bilateral proptosis with impairment of central vision of his left eye and defective color vision especially red and green. Examination revealed afferent pupillary defect of his left eye. Vision was 6/24 in right eye and 2/60 in left eye. He gave history of thyroid eye disease.

options.A: Color vision affection denotes patient should be referred to an ophthalmologist rapidly.
options.B: The cause of proptosis may be due to accumulation of fats in extraocular muscles only.
options.C: CT scan of orbit is a main tool in diagnosis.
options.D: Dry eye never occurs in thyroid eye disease.

explanations.A: Impaired colour vision, especially red-green desaturation, alongside a relative afferent pupillary defect and reduced acuity in this vignette signals compressive dysthyroid optic neuropathy, from swollen extraocular muscles crowding the orbital apex and compressing the optic nerve. This is an urgent finding that can progress to permanent vision loss without timely treatment, which is why rapid ophthalmology referral is warranted. Colour vision is a sensitive early marker of optic nerve dysfunction, often affected before visual acuity itself declines substantially.
explanations.B: The orbital crowding in thyroid eye disease is driven chiefly by extraocular muscle enlargement (inflammatory infiltration and glycosaminoglycan deposition within the muscles), not by fat accumulation alone; attributing it to fat 'only' understates the muscle involvement that CT imaging characteristically shows.
explanations.C: CT scanning of the orbit is indeed a main diagnostic tool in thyroid eye disease, but that supporting fact is not the one this key selects as the correct statement for this vignette.
explanations.D: Dry eye IS a recognised feature of thyroid eye disease, from lid retraction, lagophthalmos and tear-film instability, so a claim that it "never" occurs is false.

questions.question: A 67-year-old female came to emergency room with severe headache, vomiting and protrusion of her right eye. Examination revealed bilateral papilledema. The patient gave history of radical mastectomy for cancer breast followed by chemotherapy 2 years ago.

options.A: Proptosis may be due to metastasis.
options.B: Protrusion of the eye may be due to chemotherapy.
options.C: Bilateral papilledema denotes a localized tumor in right eye.
options.D: CT scan of the globe is recommended.

explanations.A: This patient's history of breast cancer with mastectomy and chemotherapy, together with new proptosis, headache, vomiting and bilateral papilledema, is highly consistent with orbital or intracranial metastatic spread. Metastasis is a recognised, though less common, cause of proptosis alongside thyroid eye disease, orbital cellulitis and cavernous sinus thrombosis. The combination of a known malignancy history with new orbital or raised-intracranial-pressure signs should specifically raise metastatic disease on the differential.
explanations.B: Chemotherapy is not a typical direct cause of globe protrusion; the vignette's malignancy history instead raises metastatic spread as the more relevant explanation.
explanations.C: Bilateral papilledema reflects raised intracranial pressure, a diffuse process, and does not by itself denote a tumour localised to one eye.
explanations.D: A CT scan of the orbit alone would not adequately assess this patient's likely intracranial and skull-base disease; more extensive neuroimaging, not simply "the globe," would be recommended.

This cicatricial route is a distinct mechanism from involutional entropion's simple age-related lid laxity.

questions.question: A 45-year-old female came complaining of epiphora and bad cosmetic appearance of her lower lid. She gave a history of chemical burn to her skin below lid in the last 6 months. Examination showed exposure of palpebral conjunctiva.

options.B: Shortening of skin is not the cause.
options.C: Treatment is by a skin graft.

explanations.A: A history of chemical burn to the skin below the lid, followed by epiphora, poor cosmetic appearance and exposure of the palpebral conjunctiva, is the classic presentation of cicatricial ectropion: vertical shortening of the burned, scarred skin pulls the lid margin outward. This mechanism, a skin deficit from the burn scar, distinguishes it from involutional ectropion's simple age-related lid laxity. The chemical burn history is the key clue pointing specifically to the cicatricial subtype.

explanations.C: A skin graft is indeed the definitive treatment for cicatricial ectropion, but that management detail is not the diagnostic statement this key selects as correct for this vignette.
explanations.D: Involutional ectropion is an age-related laxity condition without a burn or scarring history; it does not fit this patient's specific chemical-burn presentation as well as cicatricial ectropion does.

questions.question: A 70-year-old male came complaining of lacrimation, inability to close the lids while sleeping. Examination revealed keratitis and ulcer at lower part of cornea.

options.A: The commonest cause is Bell's palsy.
options.B: The eyes roll down during sleep.
options.C: Treatment is artificial tears and temporary lateral tarsorrhaphy.

explanations.A: Facial (7th cranial) nerve palsy is the commonest cause of lagophthalmos generally, but Bell's palsy specifically is not stated or implied in this vignette, so it is not the statement this key selects as correct here.
explanations.B: During sleep the eyes physiologically roll UPWARD (Bell's phenomenon), not downward, which is part of why lagophthalmos exposes the lower cornea specifically, matching this vignette's lower corneal ulcer; a claim that the eyes 'roll down' is therefore incorrect.
explanations.C: This elderly patient's inability to close the lids during sleep, with resulting exposure keratitis and a lower corneal ulcer, is managed with artificial tears to lubricate the exposed surface and temporary lateral tarsorrhaphy to narrow the palpebral fissure and protect the cornea while the underlying cause is addressed. This combination treats both the immediate exposure and buys time for further work-up or definitive management. Temporary, rather than permanent, tarsorrhaphy is preferred when the underlying cause may still improve.
explanations.D: Proptosis (as in thyroid eye disease) can indeed lead to lagophthalmos by preventing full lid closure over a forward-displaced globe, but that general association is not the specific management statement this key selects as correct for this vignette.

questions.title: A 30-year-old female came to ophthalmic clinic with upper lid diffuse edema after putting a new type of cosmetics. The lid was red hot and swollen.
questions.question: A 30-year-old female came to ophthalmic clinic with upper lid diffuse edema after putting a new type of cosmetics. The lid was red hot and swollen.

options.A: Lid edema may be due to mosquito bite.
options.B: Bilateral lid edema maybe due to renal or cardiac diseases.
options.C: Acute hordeolum never causes lid edema.
options.D: Lid edema cannot happen due to spread of fluid from scalp or face.

explanations.A: An insect bite is indeed a recognised local cause of lid oedema, but that fact about a different trigger is not the statement this key selects as correct for this cosmetic-related vignette.
explanations.B: Bilateral lid oedema can indeed be a sign of underlying renal or cardiac disease, since the eyelid's loose connective tissue is a classic site for early systemic fluid accumulation (from fluid overload or hypoalbuminaemia) to become visible. This is an important systemic red flag to consider whenever lid swelling is bilateral and otherwise unexplained, distinguishing it from this vignette's unilateral, cosmetic-triggered, allergic presentation. Recognising this distinction guides whether local allergy management or a systemic work-up is more appropriate.
explanations.C: Acute hordeolum CAN cause localised lid oedema from the surrounding inflammatory response, so a claim that it "never" does is incorrect.
explanations.D: Lid oedema CAN spread into the loose eyelid tissue from adjacent scalp or facial infection or inflammation, since the eyelid skin has no deep fascial barrier to stop such spread, so a claim that it "cannot" happen is incorrect.

questions.question: A patient came complaining of left epiphora. She gave history of an accident where left lid was wounded and repaired at the medial canthus. Globe was normal.

options.A: Possible cause of this condition is congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction.
options.B: Fluorescein dye disappearance test is helpful in diagnosis.
options.C: Punctal or canalicular obstruction may be the cause.
options.D: Treatment with artificial tears is the only line for treatment.

explanations.A: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction would not newly appear after an adult lid injury; it is a condition present from infancy, not one caused by adult trauma.
explanations.B: The fluorescein dye disappearance test is indeed a useful diagnostic tool, but that investigative detail is not the causation statement this key selects as correct for this vignette.
explanations.C: Epiphora developing after a lid laceration repaired at the medial canthus, where the canaliculi and puncti run close to the surface, most plausibly reflects direct injury to, or resulting obstruction of, the punctum or canaliculus at the time of the original trauma. This location-specific mechanism fits the history far better than a congenital anomaly would in an adult with a previously normal, uninjured eye. Canalicular injury near the medial canthus is a well-recognised complication of lid lacerations in this region.
explanations.D: Artificial tears may offer symptomatic relief, but they do not correct an underlying structural punctal or canalicular obstruction, so they are not "the only line" of treatment.

questions.title: A 62-year-old male came to ophthalmology clinic complaining of swelling at inner canthus. The swelling was painful and tender. Regurge was absent.
questions.question: A 62-year-old male came to ophthalmology clinic complaining of swelling at inner canthus. The swelling was painful and tender. Regurge was absent.

options.A: Most probable diagnosis is chronic dacryocystitis.
options.B: Staphylococcus aureus or streptococcus may be the cause.
options.C: Treatment by DCR is the main line of treatment.
options.D: Predisposing cause to that condition is cataract surgery.

explanations.A: Chronic dacryocystitis typically presents with a longer-standing, less acutely painful swelling and a POSITIVE regurge test, unlike this vignette's acutely painful, tender swelling with an absent regurge, which better fits acute dacryocystitis with the sac abscessed and its lumen not freely refluxing.
explanations.B: A painful, tender swelling at the inner canthus with an absent regurge test (the abscessed sac's contents not freely refluxing back through the puncti) is consistent with acute dacryocystitis, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus or streptococcal species. This organism profile guides the systemic antibiotic choice for the acute infective episode. The absent regurge in the acute setting, unlike the positive regurge typical of quiescent chronic dacryocystitis, reflects the acutely inflamed, less compressible state of the sac.
explanations.C: Dacryocystorhinostomy is the definitive procedure for chronic, not acute, dacryocystitis; treating the acute painful infection first with antibiotics is the priority before considering elective surgery.
explanations.D: Cataract surgery is a recognised predisposing factor for post-operative endophthalmitis in a patient with pre-existing chronic dacryocystitis, but that association is not the diagnostic/organism statement this key selects as correct for this acute-presentation vignette.

questions.title: A 58-year-old female came to outpatient clinic complaining of tearing and recurrent mucoid discharge. On examination a swelling below the medial palpebral ligament was detected. Regurge test was positive.
questions.question: A 58-year-old female came to outpatient clinic complaining of tearing and recurrent mucoid discharge. On examination a swelling below the medial palpebral ligament was detected. Regurge test was positive.

options.A: Positive regurge test is of no value in diagnosis.
options.B: Recurrent conjunctivitis is one of the complications of the disease.
options.C: Most probable diagnosis is acute dacryocystitis.
options.D: Inflammation of lacrimal sac is due to nasolacrimal duct obstruction.

explanations.A: A positive regurge test is highly informative in this vignette, localising the problem to the sac-to-duct level; it is not "of no value" in diagnosis.
explanations.B: Recurrent conjunctivitis, from the chronically infected reservoir seeding the ocular surface, is indeed a genuine complication of chronic dacryocystitis, but it is not the specific causation statement this key selects as correct for this vignette.
explanations.C: This vignette's tearing, recurrent mucoid discharge, medial swelling and positive regurge test together fit chronic, not acute, dacryocystitis; acute dacryocystitis is typically more acutely painful and tender rather than presenting with a longer-standing, recurrent, mucoid pattern.
explanations.D: Tearing, recurrent mucoid discharge, a swelling below the medial palpebral ligament and a positive regurge test together describe chronic dacryocystitis, in which nasolacrimal duct obstruction leads to a chronically infected, distended lacrimal sac. This underlying nasolacrimal duct obstruction is the root cause driving both the sac's inflammation and the tear-outflow failure producing epiphora. Recognising this obstruction as the cause, rather than a coincidental finding, is what guides definitive treatment toward bypassing the duct (dacryocystorhinostomy) rather than merely treating symptoms.

questions.title: A farmer came to outpatient clinic complaining of burning sensation, excessive tears and discomfort which increases while working outdoors in sun. On examination conjunctival scarring, PTDs and Arlt’s line were detected.
questions.question: A farmer came to outpatient clinic complaining of burning sensation, excessive tears and discomfort which increases while working outdoors in sun. On examination conjunctival scarring, PTDs and Arlt’s line were detected.

options.A: Cause of this condition is Sjogren's syndrome.
options.B: Mucin deficiency is the main cause.
options.C: BUT (tear film break up time) is not essential in diagnosis.

explanations.A: Sjögren's syndrome is a systemic autoimmune sicca condition, not specifically linked to prolonged outdoor sun and wind exposure in a farmer; the conjunctival scarring, pterygium-like PTDs (pinguecula/pterygium-type degenerations) and Arlt's line (a trachoma-associated tarsal conjunctival scar) in this vignette instead point to chronic environmental/cicatricial exposure, not Sjögren's.
explanations.B: This farmer's chronic outdoor sun exposure, conjunctival scarring, PTDs and Arlt's line (a linear scar in the upper tarsal conjunctiva classically from chronic trachoma) together reflect cicatrizing conjunctival disease causing goblet-cell loss and mucin deficiency. Mucin deficiency, rather than a primarily aqueous problem, is therefore the main mechanism of this patient's dry eye. This cicatricial, environmental-exposure pattern is a recognised alternative route to dry eye distinct from the autoimmune, aqueous-deficient route seen in Sjögren's syndrome.
explanations.C: Tear film break-up time IS a useful and relevant diagnostic test for this presentation, particularly given the mucin-deficiency mechanism; a claim that it is "not essential" understates its diagnostic value here.
explanations.D: Artificial tears offer symptomatic relief, but that general treatment fact is not the causation statement this key selects as correct for this vignette.

questions.title: Regarding proptosis:
questions.question: Regarding proptosis:

options.B: The distance between lateral orbital margin and corneal apex is normally 12-15 mm.
options.C: Direction of proptosis is not important.
options.D: Proptosis can be generally classified into inflammatory and neoplastic.

explanations.A: Proptosis is measured with an exophthalmometer (classically the Hertel instrument), which quantifies the distance from the lateral orbital margin to the corneal apex. This objective measurement allows serial comparison over time and side-to-side comparison for asymmetry, both clinically important in monitoring conditions like thyroid eye disease. It is the standard clinical tool for this purpose.
explanations.B: Normal exophthalmometry readings are generally lower than the 12-15mm range stated here (typically around 12-21mm depending on ethnicity and measurement technique, with substantial normal variation), so this specific figure is not the statement this key selects as correct.
explanations.C: The direction of proptosis (axial versus non-axial displacement) IS clinically important, since it helps localise the lesion to within or outside the muscle cone, so a claim that direction "is not important" is incorrect.
explanations.D: Proptosis causes are broadly classified in more ways than simply inflammatory and neoplastic (vascular and structural/traumatic causes exist too), so this narrower two-category claim is not the statement this key selects as correct.

questions.title: The commonest cause of unilateral proptosis in adults is:
questions.question: The commonest cause of unilateral proptosis in adults is:

explanations.A: Cavernous haemangioma is the commonest BENIGN orbital tumour causing proptosis, but it is not the single commonest cause of unilateral proptosis in adults overall, since thyroid eye disease outweighs it in prevalence even when presenting unilaterally.
explanations.B: Grave's disease (thyroid eye disease) is the commonest cause of unilateral, as well as bilateral, proptosis in adults, since imaging often reveals subclinical bilateral orbital involvement even when the clinical presentation appears one-sided. Its autoimmune orbital process, driving both extraocular muscle enlargement and fat expansion, accounts for its high prevalence relative to any single tumour type. This is why thyroid eye disease, not a specific orbital tumour, tops the differential for adult unilateral proptosis.
explanations.C: Neurofibroma is a recognised but much less common cause of unilateral proptosis than thyroid eye disease.
explanations.D: Metastasis is a recognised but much less common cause of unilateral proptosis than thyroid eye disease.

questions.question: The commonest benign orbital tumor causing proptosis is:

explanations.A: Cavernous haemangioma, a slow-growing, well-encapsulated vascular malformation typically within the muscle cone, is the commonest benign orbital tumour causing proptosis in adults. questions.question: Cicatricial ectropion is treated by:

explanations.A: Horizontal lid shortening addresses excess lid laxity, the mechanism of involutional ectropion, not the vertical skin shortening that drives cicatricial ectropion.
explanations.B: Levator muscle resection is a ptosis operation, addressing lid elevation, not a treatment for ectropion of any type.
explanations.C: Cicatricial ectropion follows vertical shortening of the anterior lamella (skin), most often from a burn, chronic dermatitis or a poorly healed laceration, pulling the lid margin outward as the scar contracts. Because the underlying problem is a genuine skin deficit rather than lid laxity, its definitive treatment is a skin graft, which releases the scar's tension and replaces the missing tissue. This distinguishes its management from involutional ectropion, treated by horizontal lid-shortening instead.
explanations.D: Lateral tarsorrhaphy narrows the palpebral fissure for exposure protection (as in lagophthalmos); it does not correct the underlying cicatricial skin deficit causing ectropion.

questions.title: Regarding muscles of the lid:
questions.question: Regarding muscles of the lid:

options.A: The levator palpebrae muscle is responsible for closing the lid.
options.B: Facial nerve is the nerve responsible for lid closure.
options.C: Orbicularis occuli is responsible for lid opening.
options.D: Oculomotor nerve supplies the orbicularis occuli muscle.

explanations.A: The levator palpebrae muscle OPENS the lid; it is orbicularis oculi that closes it, so this statement has the muscle-function pairing reversed.
explanations.B: The facial (7th cranial) nerve supplies orbicularis oculi, the muscle responsible for eyelid closure, which is why facial nerve palsy classically produces lagophthalmos (a closure failure). This is the opposite pairing from the oculomotor nerve, which supplies the levator palpebrae superioris for lid OPENING, so oculomotor palsy instead produces ptosis. Keeping the closing (facial/orbicularis) and opening (oculomotor/levator) pairs distinct is a fundamental point in lid-muscle anatomy.
explanations.C: Orbicularis oculi is responsible for lid CLOSING, not lid opening, so this statement has the muscle's function reversed.
explanations.D: The oculomotor nerve supplies the levator palpebrae superioris (lid opening), not orbicularis oculi (lid closing, supplied by the facial nerve), so this statement has the nerve-muscle pairing incorrect.

questions.title: Treatment of congenital ptosis:
questions.question: Treatment of congenital ptosis:

options.A: All cases should be treated as early as possible to achieve good results.
options.B: Levator muscle resection is done if levator action is poor.
options.C: Amblyopia may occur in severe unilateral cases.
options.D: Frontalis suspension is done in mild cases.

explanations.A: Congenital ptosis is not treated "as early as possible" in every case; timing is instead guided by severity, with milder cases often deferred until the child is older and better able to cooperate with a stable procedure.
explanations.B: Levator muscle resection being reserved for poor levator action somewhat understates the nuance (resection actually needs SOME levator function present to work), so this is not the most accurate statement among the options.
explanations.C: Severe unilateral congenital ptosis that occludes the visual axis risks deprivation amblyopia in the affected eye, since the developing visual system needs unobstructed, focused input during the critical period of visual maturation. This risk is why severe unilateral cases, unlike milder or bilateral cases, need closer monitoring and often earlier surgical intervention despite ptosis timing generally being individualised by severity. Recognising amblyopia risk is the central reason severe unilateral ptosis cannot simply be deferred like milder cases can.
explanations.D: Frontalis suspension, which harnesses the frontalis muscle when levator function is absent, is reserved for SEVERE cases, not mild ones, where levator function is more likely to still be present and a smaller procedure may suffice.

questions.title: The lacrimal drainage system consists of the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: The lacrimal drainage system consists of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: The puncti are a genuine part of the lacrimal drainage system, the entry points for tears into the canaliculi, so they belong among the true drainage structures, not the exception.
explanations.B: The canaliculi are a genuine part of the lacrimal drainage system, carrying tears from the puncti to the sac, so they belong among the true drainage structures, not the exception.
explanations.C: The lacrimal sac is a genuine part of the lacrimal drainage system, collecting tears before they pass down the nasolacrimal duct, so it belongs among the true drainage structures, not the exception.
explanations.D: Goblet cells are secretory structures, producing the tear film's mucin layer, not part of the excretory drainage pathway that carries tears away from the eye. Among the puncti, canaliculi and lacrimal sac, all genuine drainage structures forming one continuous outflow pathway, goblet cells are the one option that does NOT belong. This is exactly the exception the question asks for.

questions.title: Complications of chronic dacryocystitis include the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: Complications of chronic dacryocystitis include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Acute dacryocystitis, as a flare of the chronic infected sac, is a recognised complication of chronic dacryocystitis, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.
explanations.B: Recurrent conjunctivitis, seeded by the chronically infected reservoir, is a recognised complication of chronic dacryocystitis, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.
explanations.C: Glaucoma (raised intraocular pressure with optic nerve damage) is not a recognised complication of chronic dacryocystitis, a lacrimal drainage-system infection with no established mechanism for raising intraocular pressure. Among acute exacerbation, recurrent conjunctivitis and post-cataract endophthalmitis, all genuine complications arising from the chronically infected sac, glaucoma is the one condition that does NOT belong. This is exactly the exception the question asks for.
explanations.D: Endophthalmitis following cataract surgery, from the chronically colonised sac seeding the eye during intraocular surgery, is a recognised complication of chronic dacryocystitis, so it belongs among the true complications, not the exception.

questions.title: Clinical picture of chronic dacryocystitis includes the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: Clinical picture of chronic dacryocystitis includes the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Epiphora is a genuine feature of chronic dacryocystitis, from the obstructed drainage pathway, so it belongs among the true clinical picture, not the exception.
explanations.B: Swelling below the medial canthus, over the distended sac, is a genuine feature of chronic dacryocystitis, so it belongs among the true clinical picture, not the exception.
explanations.C: Recurrent mucoid discharge is a genuine feature of chronic dacryocystitis, from the chronically infected sac, so it belongs among the true clinical picture, not the exception.
explanations.D: Chronic dacryocystitis characteristically produces a POSITIVE, not a negative, regurge test: pressing the sac reflux mucoid material through the puncti, confirming the sac is patent to the puncti but obstructed at the nasolacrimal duct. Among epiphora, medial canthal swelling and recurrent mucoid discharge, all genuine features, a negative regurge test is the one statement that does NOT belong in the expected clinical picture. This is exactly the exception the question asks for.

questions.title: Treatment of acute dacryocystitis is:
questions.question: Treatment of acute dacryocystitis is:

explanations.A: Dacryocystorhinostomy is the definitive treatment for chronic dacryocystitis once inflammation has settled, not the treatment for an acute infective flare.
explanations.B: Probing is a treatment approach used for congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction in infants, not for adult acute dacryocystitis.
explanations.C: Acute dacryocystitis, an infective flare of the lacrimal sac, is managed with systemic antibiotics to control the infection together with hot fomentation to encourage localisation and comfort, reserving surgery (dacryocystorhinostomy) for once the acute inflammation has settled. This staged approach, treat the infection first and operate later, avoids operating on acutely inflamed, friable tissue. It mirrors the same acute-versus-elective principle used across other acute infective lacrimal presentations.
explanations.D: Intubation (silicone tube placement) is a technique used for canalicular or duct stenosis, not the first-line treatment for an acute infective dacryocystitis flare.

questions.title: Dry eye can be caused by the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: Dry eye can be caused by the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Obstruction of the lacrimal puncti blocks tear drainage and causes epiphora (excess tearing), the clinical opposite of dry eye, rather than dryness itself. It is therefore not a recognised cause of dry eye, which is exactly what the question asks for. This is the same drainage-versus-production/stability distinction that separates epiphora from dry eye throughout this topic.
explanations.B: Rheumatoid arthritis, a collagen-vascular disease, causes aqueous-deficient dry eye through lacrimal gland infiltration, so it belongs among the true causes, not the exception.
explanations.C: Chronic trachoma's cicatrizing conjunctival disease causes goblet-cell loss and mucin-deficient dry eye, so it belongs among the true causes, not the exception.
explanations.D: Vitamin A deficiency causes mucin-deficient dry eye through goblet-cell loss, so it belongs among the true causes, not the exception.

questions.title: A positive regurge test is diagnostic of:
questions.question: A positive regurge test is diagnostic of:

explanations.A: Punctal occlusion would prevent tears from reaching the sac at all, rather than producing the sac-reflux that a positive regurge test relies on.
explanations.B: Canalicular obstruction, proximal to the sac, would likewise prevent tears from reaching the sac to be regurgitated.
explanations.C: A positive lacrimal regurgitation test, in which pressure over the sac reflux material back through the puncti, confirms the sac is patent to the puncti but obstructed distally, localising the block to the nasolacrimal duct. This distal, sac-to-nose localisation is precisely the finding expected in chronic nasolacrimal duct obstruction. The test's underlying mechanism, forcing trapped sac contents backward because their forward route through the duct is blocked, is what makes this localisation reliable.
explanations.D: Ectropion is an eyelid-margin malposition, unrelated to the mechanism a regurge test assesses.

questions.title: The following test is used for diagnosis of dry eye:
questions.question: The following test is used for diagnosis of dry eye:

explanations.A: The fluorescein dye disappearance test assesses lacrimal drainage function, not dry eye, so it is not the test this key selects.
explanations.B: Tear break-up time, the interval before the tear film first disrupts after a blink, directly assesses tear film stability and is shortened in dry eye, particularly the mucin-deficient and evaporative forms. It is a standard, widely used diagnostic test for dry eye. A short break-up time supports the diagnosis alongside Schirmer's test and ocular surface staining.
explanations.C: Lacrimal syringing tests drainage-pathway patency, not dry eye, so it is not the test this key selects.
explanations.D: The regurge test assesses lacrimal sac and drainage-pathway patency (as in dacryocystitis), not dry eye, so it is not the test this key selects.

questions.title: Main line of treatment in acquired nasolacrimal obstruction in adults is:
questions.question: Main line of treatment in acquired nasolacrimal obstruction in adults is:

explanations.A: Systemic IV antibiotics treat an acute infective flare, not the definitive, main-line treatment for acquired nasolacrimal obstruction itself.
explanations.B: Nasolacrimal duct massage is used for CONGENITAL nasolacrimal duct obstruction in infants, where the duct may still open spontaneously, not for acquired obstruction in adults.
explanations.C: Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR), surgically connecting the lacrimal sac to the nasal cavity to bypass the obstructed nasolacrimal duct, is the standard, definitive treatment for acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction in adults. Because the obstruction in adults is typically a fixed anatomical narrowing rather than a developmental one likely to resolve on its own, surgical bypass rather than conservative massage is the appropriate main-line approach. This is the same DCR procedure used for chronic dacryocystitis once inflammation has settled.
explanations.D: Intubation (silicone tube placement) is used for partial stenosis or as an adjunct, not as the main line of treatment for established acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction.
